title: Chapter 30 — Working Multiple Customers and Floor Craft
intro: The Saturday skill — managing several live customers with grace, timing, and team discipline.

sections.title: The Saturday Problem
sections.content:
On a busy Saturday, you will have three customers at different stages of the 10 Steps at the same time. One just walked in. One is in the middle of a demo. One is ready to close.

If you focus entirely on one, you lose the other two. If you bounce between all three without structure, you give everyone a mediocre experience.

Floor craft is the skill of managing multiple customers simultaneously without any of them feeling abandoned or rushed.

sections.title: The Handoff Is a Skill
sections.content:
You cannot be in three places at once. But you can manage transitions.

When you need to step away from a customer, tell them exactly what is happening and exactly when you will be back. 'I want to check on something for you. Give me three minutes and I will be right back with that delivery information.'

That is respectful. It sets expectations. And it gives you time to check on your other customer.

If you need to pass a customer to a teammate, do it with a proper introduction — not a cold handoff. 'This is Sarah — she knows everything about laundry and she is going to take excellent care of you while I finish up with another customer.' That is a warm transfer. The customer feels valued, not abandoned.

sections.title: Team Selling
sections.content:
On a busy floor, individual heroics are less important than team coordination. The best stores have salespeople who help each other without keeping score.

If you see a teammate drowning with three customers and you have none, step in. Not to steal the sale — to help the customer. The team that wins together earns together. Floor craft is not a solo sport.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating floor craft, ask:

Can the salesperson manage multiple customers without anyone feeling ignored?
Do they communicate clearly when stepping away — setting expectations for their return?
Do they hand off customers professionally when needed?
Do they support teammates on busy days — or only focus on their own sales?

Floor craft separates the professionals from the amateurs. Anyone can sell one customer at a time. Managing three at once while delivering a great experience to all of them — that is the skill.
